image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the temperature records set in the year 2021. The annual temperature records from 1991 to 2020 are also displayed. In recent years, I believe climate change has had a considerable impact on US temperatures. In 2002, the United States experienced a severe heatwave, followed by another in 2020. Given that the data in 2019 were nowhere near what they are now, I'm curious as to why there was such a sudden rise in temperatures. I'm interested to see how the climate and temperature will change in the future. This affects my community because global warming affects the enivormient in which we live in.  I would title this graph "Extreme Recordbreaking Tempetures".

I'm a newbie to this site, but here are my general reactions:

1. This Weather  (short term) bar chart is interesting, but your animated 1920-present time series graphs (of shifting of night time temps in this case) in various cities are very cool, and much more relevant to increasing climate change hazards, and whatever clues that provide for underlying mechanisms and tipping points.  

I also like the national maps of T and pressure anomalies, which show a more nuanced level of changes. 

See Sept 13 article, Why We’re Experiencing So Many Unusually Hot Summer Nightshttps://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/09/13/upshot/up-hot-nights.html2. Re: heat and cold stress to humans, biomes, the grid etc:  please include metric that adjusts for humidity, wind, radiant T, etc., such WBGT, Heat Index.  Relying on T only can be misleading, especially for extreme events.

3. I also like the Synoptic System weather maps, 
which include the most hazardous  hot types: Moist Tropical, and Dry Tropical.  We need to track the changes in the SW monsoon that can also affect S. California. 

See tables and maps by Sheridan et al at Kent State U. 
The animated maps of system types around the globe are especially cool:http://sheridan.geog.kent.edu/ssc3.html, 2021 and historical trend maps

Typo: you did not say what metric was for the record T. Daily max, daily min, monthly max or what? Also, it would be good to show historical avg or median at same time.

What do you notice?
When looking at this graph, I read the headline first to understand what I am looking at. The sub header reading "All-time temperature records were set in 2021 at 10.6 percent of all US stations" provides the most insight to me. From there, I see that most of the temperature records were referring to hottest days rather than cold because of the colors of the first and second graphs. But, from there I see that a majority of the heat records were mostly set in the north west corner whereas the cold records were set in the mid west. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder if these heat records in the north west are out the ordinary. Is this area usually cold and now its suddenly hot or was it always rather hot but just hotter now? I also wonder if these graphs/statistics are being taken to prove climate change or to disprove climate change. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
Being since I live in New Jersey, this graph does not entirely relate to me, for it doesn't show any temperature records being broken in my state. But, this does relate to my larger community, my country, for we need to collect info like this to learn from it.

This could be accredited to climate change as over the years the earth becomes hotter, so fewer cold temperature records are being broken. We can see on the second graphic that these record temperatures are being broken in 2021. For the most part the majority of these heat record are recorded in the upper northwest. Around a dozen are spread out across the southwest. The cold record temperatures are recorded in the middle of the United States. Some of the largest are recorded in Texas, which I would not normally think would be a place for cold temperature records. The graph also shows when the hot and cold records occurred. For heat, they occurred in June in a heatwave. For the cold, they occurred in February during a cold snap. A good name for this graph would be "Temperature Records in the United States and The History".

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing that I noticed in the graph was the June heat wave happening in the Pacific Northwest, or Oregon, Washington, and parts of Idaho and California. There are also spots in Utah, Nevada, and Colorado. I think this probably occurred because of the wildfires that were happening out west last June due to drought and lack of moisture. Conversely, states in the midwest seemed to get colder, such as in Texas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas. I recall the massive blizzard and cold snap that occurred in winter of 2021, leaving many Texans and residents of Arkansas without power or heat. I also noticed that in both scenarios, the largest "circles" are in areas that are the farthest away from the ocean. 

I wonder why certain parts of the country are experiencing more hot extreme temperatures, while others are experiencing colder extremes. More importantly, how is this possible when some of them practically overlap each other? One thing that I also wonder is how the US government is planning on responding to the growing weather extremes happening in the US. Is the a change in moisture patterns, shown by the graph? Will there be a carbon tax imposed? Sustainable energy? 

This impacts me and my community because I am a teenager who is watching climate change affect my environment in my own eyes. Eventually, when I grow up, it will be me and my generation's responsibility to help reduce or reverse climate change before it's too late.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs relate to extreme temperature records in the United States by year and by location.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 18 with moderation on Wednesday, March 23.  The topic – population dynamics.  Keep noticing and wondering.

I noticed a more consistent spike in scorching temperatures compared to colder temperatures. I also found it compelling that based on these graphs the more consistent “warmer states” recorded a massive change in temperature regarding cooler climates. And on the other end, the pacific northwest registered higher heat temperatures. I would have estimated the opposite of the final data. I wonder how long this consistency in sporadic changes in climate is sustainable not only for our country shown in this graph but also how this affects our planet at large. We have many practical steps that each individual can do, to help reduce our carbon footprint. But in reality what are the major causes for these spikes? I wonder what legislature needs to be put in place, for the major contributors to this issue in our communities to begin to make a change. I am from Portland Oregon so in my community, these spikes are not welcomed with open arms by most. People in my community are not often exposed to such heat so it caused momentary health issues and scares when high heat have occurred. When conditions are not ideal some community members were not able to go to work and with different work policies Some people unfortunately loose income because of extreme conditions which would not be healthy for them to work in.
